**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 46, verses 7–9:**

The Almighty said:

﴿When Our clear verses are recited to them, those who disbelieve say of the truth when it comes to them, "This is manifest sorcery." Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say, "If I have invented it, then you cannot avail me anything against Allah. He is most knowing of what you spread about it. Sufficient is He as witness between me and you. And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."﴾ ﴿Say, "I am not an innovation among the messengers, and I do not know what will be done with me or with you. I only follow what is revealed to me, and I am but a clear warner."﴾

The verses mentioned are the verses of the Qur'an, as evidenced by His saying ﴿"tutlā" (are recited)﴾ and the disbelievers' saying ﴿"This is manifest sorcery"﴾. They said this about the Qur'an because they said that it separates a man from his child, and from his spouse, and similar things that are found in a like manner in sorcery, in another respect.

As for His saying ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"﴾: the "am" here is a disjunctive (*maqta'a*) "am," assumed to mean "bal" (rather) together with the interrogative hamza. The word ﴿"iftarāhu" (he has invented it)﴾ means he fabricated it and made it up. So Allah, blessed and exalted, commanded him to say: "If I have invented it, then Allah is sufficient for me in that matter, and He would punish me and not give me respite." Then the speech returned to the interrogative form addressed to Allah, the Exalted, seeking His help against them, and awaiting what His knowledge requires regarding what they spread of falsehood and of rejecting the truth. That requires their punishment, so in the expression there is a threat. The pronoun in His saying ﴿"fīhi" (about it)﴾ may refer to the Qur'an, and it may refer to ﴿"mā" (what)﴾. The pronoun in ﴿"bihi" (with Him)﴾ refers to Allah, the Exalted, and ﴿"bihi"﴾ is in the nominative position. And "afāḍa al-rajul fī al-ḥadīth wa naḥwihi" (a man plunged into speech or the like) means when he delved into it and persisted. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿"and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful"﴾ is an expression of hope and an invitation to repentance, because these two attributes came in the midst of His threatening them by Allah, the Exalted.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded him to argue against them that he was not an innovation (*bid'an*) among the messengers, that is, others had come before me. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-A'raj. The words "bidaʿ" and "badī'" regarding things mean what one has not seen the like of. From this is the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

*So I am not a novelty among the events that befall men who were shaken after my misery and good fortune.*

Ikrima, Ibn Abi 'Ablah, and Abu Haywa recited ﴿"bidaʿan"﴾ with a fatha on the dal. Abu al-Fath said: the estimated meaning is "dha bida'" (possessor of novelty), so the noun in the genitive was omitted, as the poet said:

*And how can you keep in touch with one whose companionship has become like that of Abu Murahhib?*

People differed regarding His saying, the Exalted, ﴿"and I do not know what will be done with me or with you"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, Qatada, Ikrima, and al-Hasan said its meaning is: in the Hereafter. This was in the early period of Islam; then after that Allah, the Exalted, informed him that his past and future sins had been forgiven, that the believers have from Allah a great bounty, which is Paradise, and that the disbelievers are in the fire of Hell. The narration that occurred at the funeral of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un supports this: "By Allah, I do not know, though I am the Messenger of Allah, what will be done with me." In some narrations it reads "bihi" (with me). We have no proof in the hadith according to the narration "bihi." My understanding of this statement is that the final outcome had not been revealed to him, so he said, "I do not know." As for the one who dies in faith, he was informed of his salvation from the beginning of the mission. Otherwise, the disbelievers would have been able to say: "How can you call us to something whose outcome you do not know?"

Al-Hasan also said, and a group said: the meaning of the verse is: I do not know what will be done with me or with you in this world, whether I will be made victorious over you or you will be empowered over me, and similar meanings.

Another group said: the meaning of the verse is: I do not know what will be done with me or with you regarding commands and prohibitions, and what the Sharia obligates us with of its requirements. Al-Tabari related from some of them that he said: the verse was revealed concerning a matter the Prophet (ﷺ) was awaiting from Allah, the Exalted, other than reward and punishment. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that when the Prophet's (ﷺ) departure from Makkah was delayed, having seen in a dream that he was migrating to a land with palm trees and salt flats, the Muslims became anxious over the delay of that, so this verse was revealed.

As for His saying ﴿"in attabiʿu illā mā yūḥā ilayya" (I only follow what is revealed to me)﴾, its meaning is submission and disavowal of knowledge of the unseen, and standing with the function of warning of Allah's punishment, the Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 46, verse 10–11:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Say: "Have you considered: if it is from Allah, and you have disbelieved in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel has testified to its like and believed, while you have been arrogant?" Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieved said of those who believed: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it. And since they have not been guided by it, they will say, 'This is an ancient falsehood.'"﴾

This is a verse of questioning (tawqif) concerning the great danger in which they stand, in that they deny something beneficial to them, which would save them from punishment, without any proof or evidence for their denial. So the meaning is: What is your condition with Allah, the Exalted? And what do you expect from Him, when you have disbelieved in what came from Him? The answer to this questioning is omitted, its estimated form being: "Have you not then done wrong?" This omitted element is indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

As for ﴿"Have you considered"﴾ in this verse, it may be a particle of alerting (tanbih), being a word established for asking that does not require an object (maf'ul). It may also be that the clause "kana" (it was) and what it governs fills the place of its two objects (sadda masadda maf'ulayha).

People differed about the intended meaning of "the witness" (al-shahid). Al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Sirin said: this verse is Medinan, and the witness is 'Abdullah ibn Salam. The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"to its like"﴾, the pronoun in it refers back to the statement of Muhammad ﷺ about the Qur'an: that it is from Allah. Al-Sha'bi said: the witness is a man from the Children of Israel other than 'Abdullah ibn Salam who was in Mecca, and the verse is Meccan. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him, Mujahid, and a group said: the verse is Meccan, and the witness is 'Abdullah ibn Salam, and it is among the verses that contained an unseen matter which existence later made manifest. It has been narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Salam that he said: "It was revealed concerning me." Masruq ibn al-Ajda' and the majority said: the witness is Musa ibn 'Imran, peace be upon him, and the verse is Meccan. Al-Tabari preferred this view. The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"to its like"﴾ intends by "the like": the Torah. The pronoun, according to this interpretation, refers to the Qur'an, meaning: a witness from the Children of Israel came with its like and testified that it is from Allah, the Exalted. The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿"Say: Have you considered"﴾ — according to this interpretation — means by it the confirmation of Musa of the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and his giving glad tidings of him, and that is belief in him. As for the one who said the witness is 'Abdullah ibn Salam, his belief is clear, and likewise the Israelite who was in Mecca according to the saying of those who said so. Some have related that the agent of "amana" (believed) is Muhammad ﷺ, and this is from those who say the witness is Musa ibn 'Imran, peace be upon him. Then Allah, the Exalted, linked their arrogance and disbelief with the belief of this mentioned one, so their sin and error became evident.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved said of those who believed: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it."﴾ Qatada said: it is the statement of the nobles of Quraysh, meaning 'Ammar, Suhayb, Bilal and others like them from among those who embraced Islam and believed in the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Zajjaj, al-Kalbi, and others said: it is the statement of Kinana, 'Amir, and the rest of the neighboring Arab tribes, and they said that when Ghifar, Muzayna and Juhayna embraced Islam. Al-Tha'labi said: it is the statement of the Jews when 'Abdullah ibn Salam and others among them embraced Islam.

And "al-ifk" means falsehood, and they described it as "ancient" in the sense that it concerns matters long past, as when you say to a man who has related to you the news of Chosroes and Caesar: "This is an ancient narrative." It is also possible that they meant it is a falsehood that was said in former times.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 46, verses 12–15:**

The almighty and majestic Lord said:

﴿And before it was the Book of Moses, a guide and a mercy. And this is a Book confirming it in the Arabic tongue, to warn those who have wronged, and as good news for the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, there is no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise, abiding therein forever, as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents. His mother bore him with hardship and gave birth to him with hardship, and his carrying and weaning is thirty months, until, when he reaches his maturity and reaches forty years, he says, "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favour which You have bestowed upon me and upon my parents, and to do righteousness that pleases You. And make my offspring righteous for me. Indeed I have turned to You in repentance, and indeed I am of the Muslims."﴾

The pronoun in His saying ﴿"And before it"﴾ refers to the Qur'an, and ﴿"the Book of Moses"﴾ is the Torah. Al-Kalbi read *kitāb Mūsā* as *kitāba Mūsā* with a fatḥa on the bā', by supposing a verb such as "Allah sent down" or something similar. *Al-imām* (the imam) is the string used by builders to align a structure, and everything that is followed and taken as a guide is an imam. *Imāman* is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and *raḥmatan* is conjoined to *imāman*. The indication in His saying ﴿"And this is a Book"﴾ is to the Qur'an. *Muṣaddiq* means: confirming the Torah, which contained its report and the affair of Muḥammad (ﷺ), so the Qur'an came as confirmation of that report. In the codex (muṣḥaf) of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud there is: *muṣaddiqun limā bayna yadayhi lisānan*.

Grammarians differed over the accusative of His saying ﴿"in the Arabic tongue"﴾ (*lisānan*). One group of grammarians said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. Another group said *lisānan* is a tamyīz of confirmation (*tawṭi'a muʾakkida*), and *ʿarabiyyan* is a circumstantial state. Another group said *lisānan* is the object of *muṣaddiq*, and by this view the meaning of "tongue" is Muḥammad (ﷺ) and his tongue, so the Qur'an, by its inimitability and its eloquent circumstances, confirms the one who brought it. This view is sound in meaning and good, and what we mentioned earlier is also a valid direction.

Nāfi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir (according to what was transmitted from him), Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Raja', and the people read *li-tundhira* with a *tā'* (you, O Muḥammad). Abu Ḥatim preferred this reading. The rest of the readers, and al-A'mash, read ﴿"to warn"﴾ (*liyundhira*), i.e., the Qur'an. ﴿"Those who have wronged"﴾ are the disbelievers who directed worship to other than its proper object, toward idols and images. His saying ﴿"and good news"﴾ (*wa bushrā*) may be in the nominative position, conjoined to His saying ﴿"confirming"﴾ (*muṣaddiq*), and it may be in the accusative position, standing in the place of a verb, conjoined to ﴿"to warn"﴾ (*liyundhira*), meaning: "and it gives good news to the doers of good."

When He described the disbelievers as ﴿"those who have wronged"﴾, He described the believers as ﴿"the doers of good"﴾ (*al-muḥsinīn*), because of the correspondence of the word *iḥsān* (goodness) in contrast to *ẓulm* (wrongdoing). Then He informed of the good state of the believers who remain upright, and removed from them fear and grief. Many people held that the meaning of the verse is: "then they remained upright in acts of obedience and righteous deeds." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the meaning is: by persisting in faith and not deviating from it.

The judge Abu Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is more general in hope and broader. Even if among the believers in general there are those who are punished and upon whom the threat is executed, such a person is still among those who will abide forever in Paradise, and fear and grief, which befall the disbelievers, are removed from him.

*Al-khawf* (fear) is worry about what is to come, and *al-ḥuzn* (grief) is worry about what has passed. It may be used for what is to come figuratively, because one grieves over the fear of some matter. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿"there is no fear"﴾ (*fa-lā khawfa*) without tanwīn. His saying ﴿"as a reward for what they used to do"﴾: the *mā* (what) refers to the part which is the servant's acquisition (*iktisāb*). Allah, exalted is He, has made deeds signs of the servant's steadfastness, not that they obligate Allah to do anything.

His saying ﴿"And We have enjoined upon man"﴾ intends the species, i.e., this is how My laws and books have been laid down for My prophets. Thus it is a command from Allah, exalted is He, concerning His servants. The majority of readers read *ḥusnan* with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and sukūn on the sīn, and its accusative is according to the estimate: "We enjoined him to do an act of goodness," as though the verb was made to govern it as a second object. ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him), Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥman, and ʿIsā read *ḥasanan* with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and the sīn, and this is like the first. It is possible that both are verbal nouns (*maṣdar*), like *al-bakhl* and *al-buḵl* (stinginess). It is also possible that this second word is a noun rather than a verbal noun, meaning: "We obligated him with them to an act that is good." ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī read *iḥsānan*, and this is in the accusative as a pure verbal noun (*maṣdar ṣarīḥ*), and the second object is in the prepositional phrase. The *bā'* is connected either to *waṣṣaynā* (We enjoined) or to His saying *iḥsānan* (goodness).

Kindness to parents is obligatory by this verse and others. Disobedience to them is one of the major sins. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Everything between a person and Allah, exalted is He, has a veil, except the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the supplication of the parents."

The judge Abu Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

They will supplicate only if the child has wronged them. So this ḥadīth falls under the general scope of his (ﷺ) saying: "Beware of the supplication of the one who has been wronged, for there is no veil between it and Allah."

Then He enumerated the favours of mothers upon children. He mentioned the mother in this verse in four stages, and the father in one stage, and remembrance combined them in His saying ﴿"to his parents"﴾. Then He mentioned the carrying for the mother, then the giving birth for her, then the nursing which He expressed by *fiṣāl* (weaning). This corresponds to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said when he assigned three quarters of righteousness to the mother and one quarter to the father, when "a man said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, who is most deserving of my goodness?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your father.'"

His saying ﴿"with hardship"﴾ (*kurhan*) means: throughout the remaining continuation of the pregnancy, when its events are expected. It may also be understood as: at the time of carrying, since she has no warning about it, neither in its bearing nor in its abandonment. Mujahid, al-Ḥasan, and Qatada said: the meaning is: she carried him with difficulty and gave birth to him with difficulty. Most readers read *kurhan* with a ḍamma on the kāf, while Ibn Kathir, Nāfi', Abu ʿAmr, al-A'raj, and Shayba read *karhan* with a fatḥa on the kāf. Mujahid, Abu Raja', and ʿIsā read both. Abu ʿAlī said: they have the same meaning; the ḍamma form is the noun, and the fatḥa form is the verbal noun. One group said: *al-kurh* with a ḍamma means hardship, while *al-karh* with a fatḥa means overpowering and compulsion, and by this view they weakened the fatḥa reading. Some said: if it were *karhan*, she would have been compelled by it against herself, since *al-karh* is compulsion and overpowering. The view we mentioned earlier is more correct.

Most people read ﴿"and his weaning"﴾ (*wa fiṣāluhu*), because it is a construction of two parties (*mufāʿala*), as though he separated from his mother and she separated from him. The Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, and al-Jaḥdari read *wa faṣluhu*, as though it was the mother who weaned him.

His saying ﴿"thirty months"﴾ implies that the period of carrying and nursing together is this period, because in the expression there is an omitted modifier, estimated as: "and the period of his carrying and his weaning." This can only be the case if one of the two extremes is shorter. Either the woman gives birth after six months and nurses for two years, or she gives birth after nine months according to custom and nurses for two years minus a quarter of a year. If the period of carrying increases, the period of nursing decreases, and vice versa. From this it follows that the minimum period of carrying is six months, and the least a mother nurses a child is one year and nine months, while completing two years is for one who wishes to complete the nursing. This, regarding the matter of carrying, is the view of ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) and a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, and it is the view of Malik (may Allah have mercy on him).

People differed about *al-ashudd* (maturity). Al-Shaʿbi and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is puberty, when bad deeds are recorded against him and good deeds are also recorded for him. Ibn Ishaq said: eighteen years. It was also said: twenty years. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: thirty-three years. The majority of scholars of reflection said: thirty-six years. Hilal ibn Yasaf and others said: forty years. The strongest view is thirty-six. Whoever holds forty says in the verse: He, exalted is He, emphasized and explained *al-ashudd* by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿"and reached forty years"﴾. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned forty because it is the limit of a person's soundness and excellence. In a ḥadīth: "Satan drags his hand over the face of whoever has passed forty without repenting, and says: 'By my father, a face that will not prosper!'" Aymān ibn Khuraym al-Asadi said:

*When a man completes forty, and has no modesty or veil left to him beyond what comes,*
*Then leave him, and do not begrudge him what he has decided, even if life has drawn its causes to him.*

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) there is: ﴿"until, when he attains his maturity and reaches forty years"﴾ (*ḥattā idhā istawā ashuddahu*).

His saying *awzi'nī* means: push me away from obstacles and restrain me from hindrances, so that I may be grateful for Your favour. It may also mean: make my share and portion, and this comes from *al-tawzīʿ* (distribution) and *al-qawm al-awzāʿ* (the scattered people), and from your saying: "They distributed the wealth (*tawazzaʿū al-māl*)." In the codex (muṣḥaf) of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud there is: *muṣaddiqun limā bayna yadayhi lisānan*.

Grammarians differed over the accusative of His saying ﴿"in the Arabic tongue"﴾ (*lisānan*). One group of grammarians said it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. Another group said *lisānan* is a tamyīz of confirmation (*tawṭi'a muʾakkida*), and *ʿarabiyyan* is a circumstantial state. Another group said *lisānan* is the object of *muṣaddiq*, and by this view the meaning of "tongue" is Muḥammad (ﷺ) and his tongue, so the Qur'an, by its inimitability and its eloquent circumstances, confirms the one who brought it. This view is sound in meaning and good, and what we mentioned earlier is also a valid direction.

Nāfi', Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir (according to what was transmitted from him), Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Raja', and the people read *li-tundhira* with a *tā'* (you, O Muḥammad). Abu Ḥatim preferred this reading. The rest of the readers, and al-A'mash, read ﴿"to warn"﴾ (*liyundhira*), i.e., the Qur'an. ﴿"Those who have wronged"﴾ are the disbelievers who directed worship to other than its proper object, toward idols and images. His saying ﴿"and good news"﴾ (*wa bushrā*) may be in the nominative position, conjoined to His saying ﴿"confirming"﴾ (*muṣaddiq*), and it may be in the accusative position, standing in the place of a verb, conjoined to ﴿"to warn"﴾ (*liyundhira*), meaning: "and it gives good news to the doers of good."

When He described the disbelievers as ﴿"those who have wronged"﴾, He described the believers as ﴿"the doers of good"﴾ (*al-muḥsinīn*), because of the correspondence of the word *iḥsān* (goodness) in contrast to *ẓulm* (wrongdoing). Then He informed of the good state of the believers who remain upright, and removed from them fear and grief. Many people held that the meaning of the verse is: "then they remained upright in acts of obedience and righteous deeds." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) said: the meaning is: by persisting in faith and not deviating from it.

The judge Abu Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

This view is more general in hope and broader. Even if among the believers in general there are those who are punished and upon whom the threat is executed, such a person is still among those who will abide forever in Paradise, and fear and grief, which befall the disbelievers, are removed from him.

*Al-khawf* (fear) is worry about what is to come, and *al-ḥuzn* (grief) is worry about what has passed. It may be used for what is to come figuratively, because one grieves over the fear of some matter. Ibn al-Sumayfa' read ﴿"there is no fear"﴾ (*fa-lā khawfa*) without tanwīn. His saying ﴿"as a reward for what they used to do"﴾: the *mā* (what) refers to the part which is the servant's acquisition (*iktisāb*). Allah, exalted is He, has made deeds signs of the servant's steadfastness, not that they obligate Allah to do anything.

His saying ﴿"And We have enjoined upon man"﴾ intends the species, i.e., this is how My laws and books have been laid down for My prophets. Thus it is a command from Allah, exalted is He, concerning His servants. The majority of readers read *ḥusnan* with a ḍamma on the ḥā' and sukūn on the sīn, and its accusative is according to the estimate: "We enjoined him to do an act of goodness," as though the verb was made to govern it as a second object. ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him), Abu ʿAbd al-Raḥman, and ʿIsā read *ḥasanan* with a fatḥa on the ḥā' and the sīn, and this is like the first. It is possible that both are verbal nouns (*maṣdar*), like *al-bakhl* and *al-buḵl* (stinginess). It is also possible that this second word is a noun rather than a verbal noun, meaning: "We obligated him with them to an act that is good." ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī read *iḥsānan*, and this is in the accusative as a pure verbal noun (*maṣdar ṣarīḥ*), and the second object is in the prepositional phrase. The *bā'* is connected either to *waṣṣaynā* (We enjoined) or to His saying *iḥsānan* (goodness).

Kindness to parents is obligatory by this verse and others. Disobedience to them is one of the major sins. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Everything between a person and Allah, exalted is He, has a veil, except the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the supplication of the parents."

The judge Abu Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said:

They will supplicate only if the child has wronged them. So this ḥadīth falls under the general scope of his (ﷺ) saying: "Beware of the supplication of the one who has been wronged, for there is no veil between it and Allah."

Then He enumerated the favours of mothers upon children. He mentioned the mother in this verse in four stages, and the father in one stage, and remembrance combined them in His saying ﴿"to his parents"﴾. Then He mentioned the carrying for the mother, then the giving birth for her, then the nursing which He expressed by *fiṣāl* (weaning). This corresponds to what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said when he assigned three quarters of righteousness to the mother and one quarter to the father, when "a man said to him: 'O Messenger of Allah, who is most deserving of my goodness?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your mother.' He said: 'Then who?' He said: 'Your father.'"

His saying ﴿"with hardship"﴾ (*kurhan*) means: throughout the remaining continuation of the pregnancy, when its events are expected. It may also be understood as: at the time of carrying, since she has no warning about it, neither in its bearing nor in its abandonment. Mujahid, al-Ḥasan, and Qatada said: the meaning is: she carried him with difficulty and gave birth to him with difficulty. Most readers read *kurhan* with a ḍamma on the kāf, while Ibn Kathir, Nāfi', Abu ʿAmr, al-A'raj, and Shayba read *karhan* with a fatḥa on the kāf. Mujahid, Abu Raja', and ʿIsā read both. Abu ʿAlī said: they have the same meaning; the ḍamma form is the noun, and the fatḥa form is the verbal noun. One group said: *al-kurh* with a ḍamma means hardship, while *al-karh* with a fatḥa means overpowering and compulsion, and by this view they weakened the fatḥa reading. Some said: if it were *karhan*, she would have been compelled by it against herself, since *al-karh* is compulsion and overpowering. The view we mentioned earlier is more correct.

Most people read ﴿"and his weaning"﴾ (*wa fiṣāluhu*), because it is a construction of two parties (*mufāʿala*), as though he separated from his mother and she separated from him. The Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan, Abu Raja', Qatada, and al-Jaḥdari read *wa faṣluhu*, as though it was the mother who weaned him.

His saying ﴿"thirty months"﴾ implies that the period of carrying and nursing together is this period, because in the expression there is an omitted modifier, estimated as: "and the period of his carrying and his weaning." This can only be the case if one of the two extremes is shorter. Either the woman gives birth after six months and nurses for two years, or she gives birth after nine months according to custom and nurses for two years minus a quarter of a year. If the period of carrying increases, the period of nursing decreases, and vice versa. From this it follows that the minimum period of carrying is six months, and the least a mother nurses a child is one year and nine months, while completing two years is for one who wishes to complete the nursing. This, regarding the matter of carrying, is the view of ʿAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib (may Allah be pleased with him) and a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, and it is the view of Malik (may Allah have mercy on him).

People differed about *al-ashudd* (maturity). Al-Shaʿbi and Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is puberty, when bad deeds are recorded against him and good deeds are also recorded for him. Ibn Ishaq said: eighteen years. It was also said: twenty years. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: thirty-three years. The majority of scholars of reflection said: thirty-six years. Hilal ibn Yasaf and others said: forty years. The strongest view is thirty-six. Whoever holds forty says in the verse: He, exalted is He, emphasized and explained *al-ashudd* by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿"and reached forty years"﴾. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned forty because it is the limit of a person's soundness and excellence. In a ḥadīth: "Satan drags his hand over the face of whoever has passed forty without repenting, and says: 'By my father, a face that will not prosper!'" Aymān ibn Khuraym al-Asadi said:

*When a man completes forty, and has no modesty or veil left to him beyond what comes,*
*Then leave him, and do not begrudge him what he has decided, even if life has drawn its causes to him.*

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) there is: ﴿"until, when he attains his maturity and reaches forty years"﴾ (*ḥattā idhā istawā ashuddahu*).

His saying *awzi'nī* means: push me away from obstacles and restrain me from hindrances, so that I may be grateful for Your favour. It may also mean: make my share and portion, and this comes from *al-tawzīʿ* (distribution) and *al-qawm al-awzāʿ* (the scattered people), and from your saying: "They distributed the wealth (*tawazzaʿū al-māl*)." In this case, *an* (that) is an explicit object. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: "Your favour" is in monotheism. ﴿"Righteous deeds that You are pleased with"﴾ are the prayers. "Reform in the offspring" means that they become people of obedience and goodness. The meaning of this verse is that this is how a person should act, and this is Allah's command to humanity in all the laws.

Al-Ṭabari said: it is mentioned that the beginning of this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), and then it extends to those after him. His parents had embraced Islam, so this interpretation fits only if Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) hoped for the faith of his parents and saw signs of it in them. Thus this was a favour upon them, that they were not among those who were thought to have persisted in disbelief and had been sealed in it, and then their faith appeared afterwards. The view that it is general to the human species, which neither Abu Bakr nor anyone else intended, is more correct. The rest of the verse is clear, up to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"of the Muslims."﴾

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 46, verses 16–19**

Allah the Exalted says:

﴿Those are the ones from whom We accept the best of what they did and overlook their misdeeds, among the companions of Paradise, a true promise which they were promised.﴾ ﴿And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both! Do you threaten me that I will be brought forth, when generations have passed before me?" While they both call upon Allah for help, [saying], "Woe to you! Believe, for the promise of Allah is true." But he says, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has come true, among nations that passed away before them of jinn and humans. Indeed, they were losers.﴾ ﴿And for all there are degrees according to what they did, and that He may fully repay them their deeds, and they will not be wronged.﴾ (p. 621)

His saying, the Exalted, "Those" (ulā'ika) is evidence that the reference of "al-insān" (the human being) in His saying, ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (al-insān) regarding his parents﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], is to the category (al-jins). The majority of reciters read "yatagabbalu" (He accepts) with a yā' (y) and a ḍammah, as a passive verb (ʿalā binā' al-fiʿl lil-mafʿūl), and likewise "yatajāwazu" (He overlooks). Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, read both with the nūn of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama, the "we" form). "Aḥsana" (the best) is in the accusative; this is the reading of Ibn Wathhāb, Ṭalḥa, Ibn Jubayr and al-A'mash, with a variant. al-Ḥasan read "yatagabbalu" with an open yā', and "yatajāwazu" likewise, meaning Allah the Exalted. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿among the companions of Paradise﴾ means: those for whom the mercy of Allah the Exalted has preceded. His saying, ﴿a true promise﴾, is in the accusative as an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad, a verbal noun used to reinforce the preceding verb).

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both!"﴾ up to the end of the verse: "alladhī" (the one who) refers to the category, in the sense of the generality found in the preceding verse, His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And We have enjoined upon man regarding his parents﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15]. This is the view of al-Ḥasan and a group. It is likely that it had a cause (sabab) concerning a man who said this to his parents. When [the Qur'an] finished mentioning the dutiful one, it followed with mention of this disobedient one. Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said in the book of al-Ṭabarī: "It was revealed concerning this verse about a son of Abū Bakr," without naming him. Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam said: "It was revealed concerning 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him," and Qatādah said the same. That is because he was the eldest of Abū Bakr's sons, and he witnessed Badr and Uḥud with the disbelievers. He said to his father in battle:

"Nothing remains but a coat of mail and a swift steed, ∗∗∗ and a sharp blade that slays the misguided among the gray-haired."

He challenged him to single combat. He was in Mecca in a similar state of disposition, so it was said that the verse was revealed about him. It is related that Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam delivered a sermon while he was governor of Medina, calling people to pledge allegiance to Yazīd. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr said: "You have made it Heraclian: whenever Heraclius dies, another Heraclius succeeds, and whenever Caesar dies, another Caesar succeeds." Marwān said: "Seize him!" ʿAbd al-Raḥmān entered the house of ʿĀ'isha, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her. Marwān said: "This is the one about whom Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, 'Uff to you both!'﴾." ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, heard this, denied it, reviled Marwān, and said: "By Allah, nothing of the Qur'an was revealed concerning the family of Abū Bakr except my innocence, and I know concerning whom this verse was revealed." Ibn 'Abd al-Barr mentioned that the one who gave the sermon was Mu'āwiya, may Allah be pleased with him, but that is an error. The more correct view is that the verse is general, concerning the people of these characteristics, and it did not intend ʿAbd al-Raḥmān or anyone else among the believers. The decisive proof of this is His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has come true, among nations that passed away before them﴾. ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, may Allah be pleased with him, was among the most excellent of the Companions, among the heroes, and among those who had a great contribution to Islam, and his station with Marwān on the day of al-Yamāma and elsewhere suffices as a testimony.

Abū 'Amr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, and Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif read "uffin" (أُفٍّ) with a kasrah on the fā' without tanwīn (nunation). In this case it is a sign of definiteness (ʿalāmat taʿrīf). Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ibn Muḥaysin, Shibl and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd read "uffa" (أُفَّ) with a fatḥah, and this is a dialect; both kasr and fatḥ are used. Nāfi', Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, Abū Ja'far, Shayba, al-Ḥasan and al-A'raj read "uffin" (أُفِّ) with a kasrah and tanwīn, and this is a sign of indefiniteness (ʿalāmat tankīr). It is like ṣah (صَهْ, a word for silencing), and as when you ask a man to tell you a story that is not specific, you say "īhin" (إيهٍ) with tanwīn; but if the story is one specifically referred to, you say "īha" (إيهَ) without tanwīn. As for "uff" (أُفٍّ), its origin is in filth. When the Arabs saw something foul, they said "uff." Then usage transferred it to say of anything disliked in words or deeds.

Hishām, on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, and Abū ʿAmr, as is transmitted from him, read "ataʿiddāni" (أَتَعِدَانِي, with one nūn). Abū ʿAmr, Nāfi', Shayba, al-A'raj, al-Ḥasan, Abū Ja'far and the majority of reciters read "ataʿiddānninī" (أَتَعِدَانِنِي) with two nūns. The first reading is with the nūn assimilated into the nūn (idghām). Nāfi' also read "ataʿiddānī" with one nūn and with the yā' made clear (iẓhār). Abū ʿAmr, Nāfi', ʿĀṣim, Abū Ja'far, al-A'raj, Shayba, Qatāda, Abū Rajā', Ibn Wathhāb and the majority of people read "an ukhraja" (أَنْ أُخْرَجَ) with a ḍammah on the hamzah and a fatḥah on the rā'. al-Ḥasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-A'mash, Ibn Musarrif and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "an akhruja" (أَنْ أَخْرُجَ) with a fatḥah on the hamzah and a ḍammah on the rā'. The meaning is: "that I should come out from the grave for the gathering and the return." This statement of his is an interrogation with the meaning of mockery and disbelief. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and generations have passed away before me﴾ means: they perished and passed away, and none of them came out. His saying, ﴿while they both call upon Allah for help﴾, means: the two parents. It is said: "istaghathtu Allāh" and "istaghathtu bi-Allāh" have the same meaning. "Waylaka" (ويلك) is a supplication for one who is being belittled and who is being urged toward something that is hastened toward.

al-A'raj read "anna waʿda Allāhi ḥaqqun" (أنَّ وعْدَ اللهِ حَقٌّ) with a fatḥah on the hamzah, while the others read it with a kasrah. His saying, ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾, means: this statement that includes resurrection from the graves is nothing but something that the ancients inscribed in their books, meaning the laws (sharā'iʿ). The apparent wording of this verse indicates that it was revealed concerning a specific person who said this and was told this, and Allah the Exalted condemned his statements as a warning against falling into the like of them.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has come true﴾: it is evident that it refers to a category included in His saying, ﴿the one who says﴾. It is possible, if the verse is about a specific individual, that His saying, the Exalted, "ulā'ika" (those), means: the category and kind of this mentioned one are those against whom the word has come true, that is, the word of Allah the Exalted. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿among nations that passed away before them of jinn and humans﴾, implies that jinn die just as humans die, generation after generation, and a ḥadīth has come that indicates this. al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said in one of his gatherings: "The jinn do not die." Qatāda objected to him with this verse, and he fell silent.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And for all there are degrees﴾, means the good-doers and the wrong-doers. Ibn Zayd said: "The degrees of the good-doers ascend upward, and the degrees of the wrong-doers descend downward." Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān read "wa-liyuwaffiyahum" as "wa-li-tuwaffiyahum" (وَلِتُوَفِّيَهُمْ) with a tā' at the beginning, meaning the degrees. The majority of people read "wa-liyuwaffiyahum" (وَلِيُوَفِّيَهُمْ) with a yā'. Nāfi' (with a variant from him), Abū Ja'far, Shayba, al-A'raj, Ṭalḥa and al-A'mash read "wa-linuwaffiyahum" (وَلِنُوَفِّيَهُمْ) with a nūn. al-Lu'lu'ī, in the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ūd, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "wa-lanuwaffiyannahum" (وَلَنُوَفِّيَنَّهُمْ) with a first nūn, a second emphatic nūn with shaddah, and a fatḥah on the lām. Every person harvests the fruit of his deeds, whether good or evil, and He does not wrong in the recompense; rather, every matter is placed in its proper place, whether reward or punishment.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 46, verses 23–26:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿He said, "Knowledge [of it] is only with Allah, and I convey to you that with which I have been sent, but I see you to be a people who are ignorant."﴾ ﴿And when they saw it as a cloud approaching their valleys, they said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Rather, it is that which you were impatient for: a wind within which is a painful punishment,﴾ ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord. And they became such that nothing could be seen except their dwellings. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.﴾ ﴿And We had certainly established them in that wherein We have not established you, and We made for them hearing and sight and hearts. But their hearing did not avail them, nor their sight, nor their hearts at all, since they used to deny the signs of Allah; and there encompassed them that which they used to ridicule.﴾

The meaning: Hud (ʿalayhi al-salam) said to them: "This threat is not from me. The matter belongs to Allah, the Exalted, and knowledge of its time is with Him. My duty is only to convey." The majority of readers recited: ﴿"wa-ublighukum"﴾ (p-626) with a fatha on the bāʾ and a shadda on the lām. Abu Ḥatim said: Abu ʿAmr recited it throughout the Qur'an with a sukun on the bāʾ and a light lām (ukhaffifu, i.e., without shadda). ﴿"Arākum qawman tajhalūn"﴾ means: such is a matter from the command of Allah, the Exalted, and you are ignorant of the creation of your own selves.

The pronoun in ﴿"raʾawhu"﴾ may refer to the punishment, or it may refer to the visible thing that appeared over them, which is what ﴿"ʿāriḍan"﴾ explains. The ʿāriḍ is what appears in the sky of the clouds that bring rain, and from it is the verse of al-Aʿshā:

"O you who saw a cloud, I have spent the night watching it, as if the lightning in its edges were torches."

Abu ʿUbayda said: the ʿāriḍ is that which is in the horizons of the sky in the evening, then by the next morning it has spread out. It is narrated concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿"mustaqbila awdiyatihim"﴾ that these people had suffered drought for a period, and this cloud appeared to them in the form and direction from which they always received rain; it came to them from the direction of a valley of theirs which they called al-Mughith. Ibn ʿAbbas (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhuma) said: They rejoiced at it and said, "This is a cloud bringing us rain," and he (Hud) had lied about what he threatened them with. So Hud (ʿalayhi al-salam) said to them: "The matter is not as you have seen. Rather, it is that which you were impatient for, in your saying: ﴿'Then bring us what you promise us'﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22]," then he said: ﴿"a wind within which is a painful punishment."﴾ In the reading of Ibn Masʿud: "mumṭirunā, Hud said, 'Bal huwa'" with the implied element made explicit, because the reading of the majority is like His saying: ﴿"They enter upon them from every gate"﴾ [al-Raʿd: 23] ﴿"Peace be upon you"﴾ [al-Raʿd: 24], meaning: they say, "Peace be upon you."

Al-Zajjaj said: Some people recited: ﴿"bal huwa mā istuʿjiltum bihi"﴾ with a damma on the first tā and a kasra on the jīm, and ﴿"rīḥun"﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the subject in His saying "huwa mā". ﴿"Mumṭirunā"﴾ is an epithet (naʿt) of ﴿"ʿāriḍun"﴾, and it is indefinite, and its idāfa is not a true (maḥḍa) idāfa, because the implied meaning is: "bringing rain to us in the future," so it is in the ruling of separation (infiṣāl). The stories of the wind that blew upon them, and that it used to carry the litter like a locust, have already been mentioned in other surahs.

(p-627) And ﴿"tudammiru"﴾ means: it destroys; and al-dammār means destruction. From it is the verse of Jarir:

"And for them, like the young camel of Thamud, when it roared for a time, He destroyed them with destruction."

His saying ﴿"kulla shay'"﴾ outwardly implies generality, but its meaning is specificity: in everything that You commanded to be destroyed. It is narrated that this wind cast them all into the sea.

Hamza and ʿĀṣim recited: ﴿"lā yurā"﴾ with a yāʾ, in the passive form, and ﴿"masākinuhum"﴾ in the nominative. The implied meaning: "none of them is seen." The majority of reciters recited: ﴿"lā tarā illā masākinahum"﴾, meaning: you, the addressee, see none of them. [This is the reading of Ibn Masʿud, ʿAmr ibn Maymun, al-Hasan (with a variant from him), Mujahid, ʿIsa and Talha.] Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Qatada, ʿAmr ibn Maymun, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Raja' and Malik ibn Dinar recited — meaning, without disagreement from them only among those mentioned — ﴿"lā tarā"﴾ with a tā' with a dot above, damma, ﴿"illā masākinuhum"﴾ in the nominative. It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAmir, and this is like the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"As if its camel-bridle were a ... and there remained only the sinews and the boards and the tendons."

(p-628) And like His saying:

"... so there remained only the ribs, rising."

In this reading there is awkwardness. Al-Aʿmash and ʿIsa recited: ﴿"maskanahum"﴾ in the singular, which is the noun of genus; the majority recited it in the plural. The reason for the singular is to diminish and bring close the matter (taṣghīr al-shaʾn wa-taqrībuh), as He said: ﴿"Then He brings you out as a child"﴾ [Ghafir: 67].

Then the Exalted addressed Quraysh, by way of admonition, with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿"Indeed We had established them in that wherein if"﴾ — "mā" is in the sense of "alladhī" (that which), and "in" is a negative particle placed in the position of "mā" so that the wording differs, and "mā" is not joined to "mā", because the speech is as if it said: "in that which We did not establish you." The meaning of the verse: We gave them strength, wealth, and expansiveness in wealth and bodies, which We did not give you, and this punishment befell them because of their disbelief; so you are more deserving of it if you disbelieve. (p-629) A group said: "in" is conditional, and its answer is omitted, its estimate being: "in that wherein if We had established you, you would have transgressed." This is over-exactitude in interpretation (tanaṭṭuʿ fi al-taʾwīl).

Then the Exalted enumerated to them the blessings of the senses and perception, and informed that they did not avail when they were not used as they should be. The "mā" in His saying ﴿"famā aghnā ʿanhum"﴾ is negative. This is strengthened by the entry of "min" in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿"min shay'"﴾. A group said: the "mā" in His saying ﴿"famā aghnā ʿanhum"﴾ is interrogative in the sense of confirmation (taqrīr), and ﴿"min shay'"﴾ on this view is emphatic; this is contrary to the position of Sibawayh regarding the entry of "min" in an affirmative sentence.

"Ḥāqa" means: it descended and clung, and this is used for disagreeable things. The meaning: the recompense of that which they used to ridicule.

The number of them varied greatly, so I have omitted it, since there is no soundness in that. **Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah 46, verses 30–33:**

The words of the Most High:

﴿They said, "O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses, confirming what came before it; it guides to the truth and to a straight path."﴾ ﴿"O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in him; He will forgive you some of your sins and protect you from a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of God, he cannot escape on earth, and he has no protectors apart from Him. Those are in clear error.﴾ ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to bring the dead to life? Yes indeed, He is over all things capable.﴾

The meaning: these warners, when they reached their people, said: ﴿O our people, we have heard a Book revealed after Moses﴾, meaning the Great Qur'an. They specified Moses (ﷺ) for one of two reasons. Either this group followed the religion of the Jews, or they knew that Moses, peace be upon him, had mentioned Muḥammad (ﷺ) and given glad tidings of him, so they pointed to Moses, peace be upon him, from the standpoint that the matter was mentioned in his Torah. Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him and his father, said in the book of al-Thaʿlabī: they had not known the matter of ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, and therefore they said: ﴿after Moses﴾. Their saying ﴿confirming what came before it﴾ supports this. "What is before it" refers to the Torah and the Gospel. ﴿"Al-ḥaqq"﴾ and "al-ṣirāṭ al-mustaqīm" here carry closely related meanings, but since the wording differs, (and perhaps al-ḥaqq is more general), it is as if each of them may occur in places where the other does not, which makes the repetition good.

"Dāʿī Allāh" (the caller of God) is Muḥammad (ﷺ), and the pronoun in "bihi" (in Him) refers to God, the Most High. The words of the Most High ﴿He will forgive you﴾ mean: God will forgive you.

As for the saying ﴿"wa-yujirkum"﴾, it means: He will protect you and place between you and punishment a shield of His preservation, so that no punishment reaches you. The words of the Most High ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of God﴾ and the rest of the verse may be part of the speech of the warners, and may be God's speech addressed to Muḥammad (ﷺ), the purpose being to make the unbelievers hear it. The connection of the wording to this meaning comes from the saying of the jinn: ﴿respond to the caller of God﴾; when He related that, it was said: ﴿And whoever does not respond to the caller of God﴾, meaning he is in such-and-such a state. "Al-muʿjiz" is one who goes off in the earth, showing the weakness of his pursuer, who cannot reach him. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him: "wa-laysa lahum min dūnihi" with an added mīm.

The words of the Most High ﴿Do they not see﴾: the pronoun refers to the Quraysh. This is a verse of illustration and argument, because they said that bodies cannot be raised and restored, yet they themselves acknowledged that God, the Most High, created the heavens and the earth; thus the proof was established against them from their own statements. The seeing in the words of the Most High ﴿Do they not see﴾ is seeing of the heart. The majority of readers recited ﴿"wa-lam ya-ʿya"﴾ with a sukūn on the ʿayn and a fatḥa on the final yāʾ. al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "yaʿī" with a kasra on the ʿayn and a sukūn on the yāʾ, this being by elision. The bāʾ in the words of the Most High ﴿"bi-qādirin"﴾ is a superfluous emphatic particle. Since a negation preceded in the opening of the speech, the emphasis with bāʾ is good, even though what is negated is not what the bāʾ entered upon, as in your saying "mā Zaydun bi-qāʾimin" (Zayd is not standing). In place of "Do they not see", the phrase would be "Is not the One who created", and Ibn ʿAbbās, with the majority, read "bi-qādirin". al-Jaḥdarī and al-Aʿraj, with a variant reading, and ʿĪsā and ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, read "yaqdiru" with a yāʾ as an imperfect verb; Abū Ḥātim preferred this reading and considered the majority reading erroneous because of the bāʾ's awkwardness in his view. In the Muṣḥaf of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd it reads: "wa-lam yaʿi bi-khalqihinna qādirun" without a bāʾ. The word ﴿"balā"﴾ is a response after the preceding negation; it therefore affirms what was negated. The meaning: Yes, they did see that, that is, had it benefited them and entered their hearts. Then the speech resumed with the emphatic declarative statement in the words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, He is over all things capable.﴾

He said: "All the messengers, peace be upon them, are ulu al-'azm.
